Crash Course Philosophy is brought to you
by Squarespace. Squarespace: share your passion with the world. Over the centuries, the effort to craft a perfect, bullet-proof argument for the existence of God has taken many forms. There was the ontological argument of Anselm. There were the four cosmological arguments of Aquinas. And they still have their supporters. But
many modern philosophers feel that they’re simply too flawed -- too inconsistent with our scientific understanding of the universe -- to be convincing today. But there was a fifth argument posited by
Thomas Aquinas. And it was popularized several hundred years
after his time -- in the late 1700s, by the English Christian philosopher William Paley.
And this argument for God’s existence is still around today, too. In fact, it’s one
of the most popular. It’s known as the teleological argument.
You may know it as Intelligent Design. [Theme Music] To make his case for the existence of God, William Paley gave us what’s known as an argument by analogy. This form of inductive argument invites us
to consider a particular state of affairs -- let’s just call it Situation A -- about
which we’re already likely to have certain beliefs, and then likens it to Situation B,
with which we are less familiar. The idea is that, in the interest of consistency,
whatever conclusions we’ve drawn about A, we ought to draw about B as well. You can make an argument by analogy about
anything, but Paley used it to talk about God, in what’s known as the Watchmaker Analogy.
He asked us to imagine what we’d think if we found a watch on the ground. Would we imagine that the watch simply appeared randomly, spontaneously, on its own? Or would we see the complexity
of it, and notice that its parts seem to come together in a particular way in order to accomplish
a goal? If so, wouldn’t we think that the watch must have been made by someone, on purpose? Paley was arguing that the teleology demonstrated
by a watch would lead us to conclude that it was designed by an intelligent creator
with a particular end in mind. Teleological means goal-oriented, or purposeful. And we can easily pick out the teleologies
of man-made objects. Got a mug here, as an example -- it was created with a particular
teleology in mind. It was designed to hold a liquid without leaking. It’s got a handle
put here deliberately, in such a way that human fingers could easily fit into it. And
its composition is such that it’ll keep the liquid inside warm without burning the
hand that holds it. We wouldn’t assume that a coffee cup would
simply come to be, exhibiting such perfect design for its particular function, without
someone having created it that way on purpose. So, in the same way that the teleology of
a cup implies the existence of a cup maker, and that of a watch implies the existence
of a watchmaker, Paley saw teleology in the world, and assumed from that, God’s existence. He continued his analogy by comparing a watch
to a living organism. Look at the complexity of the human body.
Heart and lungs working together, producing sweat to keep ourselves from overheating,
transforming food into energy – we’re just generally amazing all around.Look at
how elements of the natural world operate according to complex laws that sustain a beautiful,
natural harmony. Paley said this couldn't possibly just have happened, any more than the design of a pocket watch could just have happened. There must be a designer. If you accept this analogy, then you agree
with Paley that, just like the purposefulness of a watch compels us to believe in a watchmaker,
the purposefulness of the world compels us to believe in a worldmaker – God. And you might think this is a fantastic argument. It might even be what motivates your own belief in God. There are lots of people who say things like sunsets and babies show them that there must be a designer-god. But some of you probably aren’t buying it
– and you know what to do! Arguments are refuted by counterarguments,
so when you want to refute an argument by analogy, you offer a disanalogy. Basically,
you demonstrate that Situation A and Situation B are dissimilar enough that the analogy doesn’t
actually work. So, to object to Paley, we have to identify
a way in which elements of the natural world – like human bodies – are relevantly dissimilar
to watches. When we’re talking about a watch, an objector might say, it obviously had a
creator. After all, we can take it apart and see clearly how the gears fit together to
move the hands and keep time. But there’s so much in the natural world that isn’t
understandable in the same way. For instance, why would God have designed our eyes to have
a blind spot? Paley responded that it doesn’t matter whether
we can understand how something was created. The point is simply that it was. He might
point out, for instance, that I actually don’t understand the inner workings of my phone.
But I still know it had a creator. Whether or not I can understand how it
was created is beside the point. Next objection: Some parts of nature seem
to be without purpose. A blind spot obviously doesn’t have any function, and neither do
nipples on a man. Paley’s response here was: Just because we don't know there's a purpose doesn't mean there isn't one. But this is a problem, too, because his whole
argument for believing in God is that you should look at the world and see purpose.
So if we see some things in the world that are working great, and really seem to have
complexity and a definite use, and others that don’t, that’s a flaw in his argument. What’s more, the absence of any obvious
purpose in things can lead people to start searching for purposes, and effectively make
them up. For instance, I could find a purpose for this finger – I could use it as a nose-picker.
It would make a good one – it’s just the right size to really get in there and dig around.
But was my finger designed to pick noses? Probably not. 20th century British philosopher
Bertrand Russell made fun of this purpose-finding tendency, by pointing out
that you could look at a bunny and form the belief that God gave it a fuzzy white tail
so hunters would have something to shoot at.

The video discusses arguments for the existence of god often presented in philosophy.  

**An Overview of Historical Arguments**

Throughout history, philosophers have proposed numerous arguments for the existence of God. While classic ontological arguments by Anselm or Aquinas' cosmological argument have their supporters, many modern thinkers see them as too flawed in light of current scientific understanding. 

Thomas Aquinas introduced a fifth  argument that was popularized several centuries later, attributed to William Paley in the late 1700s. 
This is known as the teleological argument or Intelligent Design. It relies on the notion of intentional design in complex phenomena.

**William Paley's Analogy**

Paley used an analogy when arguing for God's existence. He likened a watch to a purposeful design by its maker, making a causal link between the intricacy and the existence of a designer—the 'Watchmaker Analogy'. This argument suggests that complexity in nature points toward intentionality with specific ends. 

**The Teleological Argument in Action**

Paley used the phenomenon of a functional object like a watch to illustrate his point, asking if we would assume random occurrence for such intricate designs.  Likewise, objects created with clear designs like cups and mugs could be easily explained by an intentional designer's purpose.  Similar thinking was applied to living organisms (e.g. human body), demonstrating how their function points toward a creator.

**Critiques of the Teleological Argument** 

Critics suggest that observing natural phenomena that seem purposeful shouldn’t automatically imply the existence of God. They question the validity of this line of thought when some elements remain unexplained, such as a blind spot in our eyes or natural processes like those of plants and animals which exhibit complex regulations but appear to  simply exist without being 'designed'

**The Counterarguments and The Role of Philosophical Discussion**

Proponents of Paley's argument counter any challenges by refuting the disanalogy-method; showing a difference in structure between an object's complexity compared to another to disrupt the analogy. For instance, they may observe that the workings of a computer (e.g., phone) are challenging to understand compared to watches and other complex machinery. 


Ultimately, philosophers grapple with whether observed purposes in nature necessarily point towards God.  Others challenge such arguments through counterarguments as illustrated by Bertrand Russell's example highlighting how purposeful design can be applied even in seemingly random phenomena.

This approach is exemplified by William Paley's Watchmaker Analogy, where he argues that intricate machinery like a watch necessitates its maker.  He expanded his analogy to include living creatures, proposing the complexity of human bodies points to a deliberate designer. When confronted with elements in nature with apparent lack of purpose, such as blind spots on humans or nipples on men, proponents of these arguments argue that the presence of such complex systems requires an intelligent creator. 

Conversely, those supporting alternatives to Paley's argument utilize reasoning based on natural processes and evolution.  For example, they assert that the complexities of living organisms can be better explained through the lens of natural selection and random mutation by Darwin and others, rather than reliance on divine intervention. The ultimate success of an "explanandum" in this case relies heavily on the ability to challenge assumptions; that if we cannot fully understand how something was created then it is not necessarily proof that it cannot be. This counters Paley's argument based on our limited understanding and the presence of a creator.

Teleology, the idea that specific natural creations point towards a designer, was central to Paley's reasoning for God's existence. He believed objects like watches demonstrate intentional design by using interconnected components for a function.  

His analogy extended to life forms; he argued complex living creatures presented evidence of purposeful creation because they display efficiency and functionality. This argument rested on the idea that: 
* **Design provides clear evidence:** Complex designs, such as the functionality of a watch, necessitate a deliberate creator for a specific purpose.
* **Analogy for God's existence:**  Paley suggested witnessing an intricate watch was proof of a world created by a designer god (similar to how a watchmaker creates watch parts). 

However, this argument received several challenges:
**Counter-arguments and Refuting Paley's Logic** 

1. **Blind spots or the need for Purpose:**  Paley argued that blind spots exist because they serve some purpose by way of design. However, this reasoning is countered as it implies a creator might intentionally leave openings in designs like fingers for no apparent reason. 
2. **Randomness and Natural Selection:** The emergence of complexity through the evolution of species via natural selection offers a scientific explanation, challenging the idea of purposeful creation. 
3. **David Hume's Objections:**   Philosopher David Hume argued that flaws within design would suggest a flawed creator, citing examples like violent events, disease, or accidents as potential evidence for inconsistencies. This counter-argument highlights the incongruence between the complexities and purposefulness observed in nature, potentially suggesting a flawed creation by god.

Despite ongoing debate, Paley's philosophical arguments regarding the relationship of the world and God remain relevant. While science has furthered understanding of processes in the natural world, the idea that specific features of nature have a deliberate meaning remains at the center of such discussions.  The challenge now lies within examining whether design can explain the complexities of an intricate biological world as it appears to be today.

The teleological argument posits the existence of a divine creator based on the apparent purposefulness of the world. This argument proposes that complexity observed in nature points towards the presence of an intelligent designer, God. **Paley's Framework:** William Paley established this reasoning. He compared the intricate workings of a watch to the organized structure of the natural world as evidence for God’s creation. This theory posits that if the complex function of both are explained through design and purpose by a creator. **Counterarguments:** Several challenges against the argument emerged: * **Nature's Purpose:** Opponents point out that many parts of nature defy clear purpose. For example, blind spots don't serve any particular function and nipples on men carry no intrinsic benefit to survival. Despite their design, these aspects can cause frustration because the logic doesn’t fit with a "pre-designed" existence model. **Russell's Critique:** Bertrand Russell further criticized the tendency of humans to impose purposes upon creation. He claimed people often invent reasons for seemingly random features of nature, like a bunny's tail being a target for hunters due to its fuzziness, despite the creature having no known purpose from an evolutionary standpoint. **David Hume's Argument:** Philosopher David Hume argued against this “design-focused” explanation by highlighting the presence of flawed and illogical elements often observed in nature. His example included the prevalence of suffering like disease and natural disasters. He highlighted these flaws as evidence that the world wasn’t shaped with a creator's design from an initial creation plan. **Modern Scientific Repercussions:** Evolutionary principles and scientific explanations have challenged the teleological argument. Its validity depends on choosing probability over certainty; it is now acknowledged to be more plausible than pure chance to believe a deity may exist within this universe’s natural development. Contemporary theories like “Fine-Tuning Arguments” rely on evolutionary theory to explain, rather than deny, a deliberate and purpose-driven structure through the existence of God **Modern Defenders of Teleological Argument:** * **Richard Swinburne:** Expands upon modern teleological arguments by emphasizing the probability of design. The most probable explanation in the presence of certain events is often based on the creator's influence and design. Overall, this analysis presents a comprehensive look at key points within the teleological argument and its evolution as scientific understanding progresses through time

* **Paley’s Argument:** William Paley's theory proposed complex living organisms must have been designed by a creator since these structures are too complex for mere chance occurrence. However, this was challenged with instances like hurricanes and the prevalence of cancer-prone tissues. He didn't explain why God would deliberately leave vulnerabilities in the system or make them so specific.
* **David Hume’s Objection:**  Philosopher David Hume pointed out flaws within this argument by suggesting life's complexity raises questions about design errors on a grand scale (ex:  earth’s tilt, and the vulnerability of a human body).
   
 Modern re-interpretations of the teleological argument attempt to address these challenges. Some arguments include:

* **Swinburne's Probability Argument:** This argument suggests that the likelihood of a universe with life existing by chance rather than through God's existence is more probable. The argument states that there is a greater probability of God's existence.
* **Fine-Tuning Arguments:**  Supporters of this approach believe the fine-tuning of conditions for life on Planet Earth supports the idea that an intelligent creator was involved as if every aspect of existence had to fall perfectly into place, such as the exact composition of Earth’s atmosphere or its location relative to the sun. 

**Weaknesses and Objections**
Despite modern-day attempts at defending the teleological argument, critics propose:  
        
* **Sampling Bias:** The sole presence of one universe creates a limited scope for valid scientific probability; comparing it to another hypothetical world would be too hard to model in the real world. They suggest a single universe makes evaluating these arguments difficult as they depend on assuming existence within such environments. 

**Response**
 Despite facing significant challenges, modern philosophers strive to strengthen the teleological argument by introducing mathematical probabilities and the possibility of chance or a predetermined design. Their focus remains on proving the plausibility of God's involvement in the creation of life.

The point is: If we’re inventing purposes, rather than recognizing ones that are inherently there, then we’re the real creators of purpose in the world, not God. Basically, if you believe that God made eyes for seeing, then you also have to believe that he designed fingers as nose-pickers and rabbit tails as bullseyes, and blind spots as ways for us to get into car accidents. 

So the counterargument here is: we don’t get to just pick and choose, and say God designed the stuff we want him to have designed, and not the other stuff.  Rather than searching for disanalogies, another way Paley's argument has been countered is with an alternative explanation for Condition B. Paley says bodies are purposeful, and from there concludes that the purpose had to have been put there by an intelligent creator. But another explanation for how bodies came to have the complexity and functionality they have today is natural selection and random mutation. We can concede that the existence of a designer-god helped make sense of the origins our world in a pre-scientific age, but now we have a perfectly good scientific explanation for how the complexity of the world came about. So, who needs a watchmaker when you have evolution by natural selection? Another objection to Paley’s case came from 18th-century Scottish philosopher David Hume, who pointed out that, if we're to take the analogy seriously, we’d need to conclude that the creator that Paley posits seems to make a lot of mistakes. And not just blind spots.

Like, how about hurricanes? Or why would he make our bodies with certain tissues - like in the breast or prostate or colon - that are so incredibly prone to cancer? Why would he make umbilical cords that could wrap around a baby’s neck? Why would he make butterflies have to wait for hours, immobile, for their wings dry as soon as they come out of their chrysalis, making them easy prey for predators? Hume pointed out that the world is chock full of stuff that looks cruel, ridiculous, impractical, and contrary to life. A flawed world, he said, implies a flawed creator.

Now, the development of evolutionary biology over the past couple hundred years has taken a pretty heavy toll on the teleological argument.  But it still has many supporters, and their method of defending their view is a good model for the way the Socratic method is supposed to work. When your opponents raise objections to your theory, you need to either reject it, or modify it in a way that responds to those objections. 

So, supporters of the teleological argument set out to modify – and strengthen – their view. Here are a couple of modern responses: Contemporary British philosopher Richard Swinburne gives us a modern teleological argument with a twist of probability. He says that, even if there’s another possible explanation for the universe, we should go with the explanation that'ss most likely to be true, and say it’s simply more probable that God designed the world than that it came about through the pure chance of evolutionary processes. Likewise, another class of modern defenses of the teleological argument are collectively known as Fine-Tuning Arguments. These arguments accept the Big Bang and evolution as they exist in evidence today. They argue for the unlikely or highly improbable nature of certain life forms based on the conditions needed to facilitate them for only one world that we can see as a means to test them out. 

But, we can’t know if it was likely or unlikely this way to happen without a multi-year experiment.
